prime.problem: Plain BPE merges whatever pairs are most common, even across a word and the punctuation or space after it. The vocabulary fills up with pieces like dog., dog! and 'e ' that mix a word's meaning with whatever symbol follows it.
prime.fits: You've written get_stats, merge, the training loop and encode for a byte-level BPE. This card adds the one step real GPT tokenizers put before all of that: cutting the text into chunks that BPE is never allowed to cross.
expect: chunks and categories (letters, numbers, punctuation, whitespace)
BPE per chunk: merges can't cross an edge
the GPT-4 pattern's changes (case, 1–3 digits, newlines)
prime.goal: Predict how the GPT-2 and GPT-4 patterns chunk a string, explain why a merge can never cross a chunk edge, and say what the split costs in compression and buys in vocabulary.

attend: Where exactly in training and encoding does the chunk boundary get enforced, and why does that make cross-category tokens impossible rather than just rare?
Why does the pattern put a space on the front of a word, and what would break if the space went on the back?
What does \s+(?!\S) leave behind in a run of spaces, and which token does that protect?
Why does the split tokenizer compress Taylor Swift's page worse (2.13× vs 2.36×), and where does the regex set a hard floor on the token count?
Which GPT-4 change removes every 4-digit token from the vocabulary, and how?

must: Regex cuts text into category chunks → get_stats counts pairs inside each chunk only → no pair ever spans two chunks → no merge (and so no token) can join a word to the punctuation, digits or space beside it

Space attaches to the front of the next word ( ?\p{L}+) → ' you' is one chunk and one common token → so \s+(?!\S) stops one space early to leave that space for the word → merges like basic BPE's 'e ' or ', ' become impossible

Chunks can only be merged within, never joined → fewer merge options → worse compression (Taylor Swift: 87,339 vs 78,746 tokens, 2.13× vs 2.36×) and a floor of one token per chunk (46,196) → you trade bytes-per-token for a vocabulary spent on real words and numbers

GPT-4 caps numbers at \p{N}{1,3} → digit chunks are at most 3 long → no cl100k token has 4+ digits (GPT-2 has 288) → every long number splits into 3-digit groups from the left, e.g. 1234567 → 123|456|7
elevated: tiktoken GPT-2 leaves ' ' as three 220 tokens even though the regex hands BPE a three-space chunk → the pattern is not the whole story; GPT-2's unreleased training applied extra rules, so you can't reproduce GPT-2's vocabulary from encoder.py alone
reference: the exact GPT-2 and GPT-4 pattern strings (minbpe regex.py L18–L19)
import regex as re is needed for \p{L}/\p{N}
possessive quantifiers ?+, ++ and tiktoken's newer, equivalent stored pattern
the tiktoken ids 220 (space), 262 (three spaces in cl100k)

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, draw the pipeline text → chunks → BPE → ids for "Hello've world123 how's are you!!!?" and mark one place a merge is forbidden. Then write 3–4 sentences on what the split costs and what it buys.
checklist: the regex splits by category: letters, numbers, punctuation, whitespace, plus contractions
BPE counts, merges and encodes inside each chunk separately, then the ids are concatenated
a space rides on the front of the following word; \s+(?!\S) leaves the last space for it
cost: fewer possible merges, so worse compression (2.13× vs 2.36×) and at least one token per chunk
gain: no tokens like dog. or ', 201'; vocabulary goes to reusable pieces
GPT-4 changed case handling, capped numbers at 3 digits and changed newline handling

retrieve.q: Explain why the chunk split guarantees that no token mixes letters and digits, instead of just making it unlikely.
answer: pairs are only counted inside a chunk, so a cross-chunk pair never gets a count
a merge is only ever created from a counted pair
at encode time each chunk is encoded alone too, so even an existing merge couldn't apply across an edge

retrieve.q: Walk GPT-2's pattern through "abc 1234567" position by position: which alternative fires at each step, and what chunk does it return? Then do the same with the GPT-4 pattern.
answer: GPT-2: ?\p{L}+ takes abc; at the space, ?\p{N}+ takes ' 1234567' (space plus all digits)
GPT-4: abc, then the numbers alternative has no optional space, so ' ' becomes its own whitespace chunk
then \p{N}{1,3} fires three times: 123, 456, 7

retrieve.q: You're designing a tokenizer for a corpus that's mostly source code. Would you use the basic tokenizer or a regex split, and what would you watch for in the pattern?
answer: basic compresses better (fewer tokens per byte), which matters for context length
the split keeps identifiers, numbers and punctuation apart, so tokens are reusable across contexts
watch whitespace: indentation runs must merge (GPT-4 merges spaces, GPT-2 didn't), and newline handling decides where indents land
the contraction rule is English-specific and matters little for code

retrieve.q: GPT-2's regex yields a three-space chunk for " hello world!!!", yet tiktoken's GPT-2 gives three 220 tokens. What does that tell you about rebuilding GPT-2's tokenizer from the pattern plus BPE?
answer: the pattern allowed the merge; the vocabulary never learned it (no 2- or 3-space token among 50,257)
so extra, unpublished rules were applied during OpenAI's training
encoder.py is inference-only, so the pattern plus BPE alone won't reproduce GPT-2's merges

compare.q: The basic training loop runs get_stats on one long id list; the regex version runs it on a list of chunks. What exactly changes in the loop, what does it change in the learned merges, and when would you choose each?
answer: the loop is the same; stats are summed over chunks and merge is applied per chunk
basic learns cross-category merges like 'e ', ', ', '. Retrieved '; regex learns er, 20, in
basic when raw compression is all that matters; regex for a general-purpose LLM vocabulary
basic fails by wasting slots on word+punctuation combos; regex fails on text its pattern handles badly (non-English apostrophes, odd whitespace)

compare.q: GPT uses a regex pre-split over bytes; Llama 2's sentencepiece uses no regex. What does sentencepiece rely on instead, and how does each approach fail on text it wasn't designed for?
answer: sentencepiece runs BPE on code points with options like split_digits, byte fallback and a dummy prefix, not a hand-written regex
a regex is explicit and easy to read but English-leaning (contractions, ASCII apostrophe)
sentencepiece's behaviour is spread over many config flags, and a wrong one (e.g. no byte fallback) silently produces <unk>

predict.q: Using GPT-4's pattern, how many chunks does "We'RE 12345 dogs... ok?" split into, and does GPT-2's pattern give more chunks, fewer, or the same?
predict.answer: GPT-4: 9 chunks, We | 'RE | ␣ | 123 | 45 | ␣dogs | ... | ␣ok | ?. GPT-2: 8 chunks, We | ' | RE | ␣12345 | ␣dogs | ... | ␣ok | ?. GPT-2 misses the uppercase contraction (so 'RE becomes two chunks) but keeps the space and all five digits in one number chunk; GPT-4 does the opposite on both. In cl100k tokens it's 9 either way, one per chunk.

apply.task: Copy labs/regex-presplit.py and add a third pattern: GPT-4's, but with \p{N}{1,3} changed to \p{N} (one digit per chunk, the way Llama's split_digits treats numbers). Run all three patterns on "abc 1234567" and on the year "2024", and count chunks.
apply.done: Your one-digit pattern gives ['abc', ' ', '1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', '7'] (9 chunks) where GPT-4 gives 5 and GPT-2 gives 2, and "2024" becomes 4 chunks where GPT-4 gives ['202', '4'].
apply.hint: The only change is dropping {1,3}. Print len(re.findall(...)) next to each list.
